notes.meaning: After Joshua died, Israel had no single human leader to take his place. The tribes turned to the Lord to ask who should lead the next attack against the Canaanites. They sought God's guidance through the high priest and the sacred lots called the Urim and Thummim. When facing new seasons and challenges, God's people do well to ask Him for direction first.

The Lord chose the tribe of Judah to lead the way into battle. Judah was the largest, strongest, and most honoured tribe, fulfilling Jacob's ancient blessing. God also gave a clear promise that He had already handed the land over to them. His call to action always comes with the strength and assurance needed to obey.

Judah asked the tribe of Simeon to join forces with them in clearing out the enemies. The two tribes were close brothers, and Simeon's allotted land lay right inside the border of Judah. They agreed to stand together and help each other secure their inheritances. Believers are called to support and strengthen one another in life's battles.

Judah marched out with Simeon, and the Lord granted them victory over their enemies. They fought against the Canaanites and Perizzites at a place called Bezek. Ten thousand enemy soldiers fell in that single battle. The victory belonged to God, who kept His promise to fight for His people.

At Bezek, the Israelite soldiers encountered the local ruler, Adoni-bezek. His title means 'lord of Bezek,' and he was a powerful local king. The men of Judah attacked his army and defeated both the Canaanites and Perizzites stationed there. God showed that even the most feared earthly leaders cannot stand against His purpose.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars suggest Adoni-bezek may be another name or title for Adoni-zedek, the king of Jerusalem mentioned in the book of Joshua.

notes.meaning: Adoni-bezek tried to escape from the battlefield, but the soldiers of Judah chased and captured him. They cut off his thumbs and big toes. This harsh punishment kept him from ever holding a sword or running into battle again. It disabled a cruel tyrant so he could no longer wage war or terrorise others.

Adoni-bezek admitted that he had inflicted this exact cruelty on seventy other kings. He had forced those rulers to grovel like dogs for food under his royal dining table. Even this pagan king recognized that God was giving him the exact punishment he had dealt to others. They took him to Jerusalem, where he eventually died.

differ.view: Letting Adoni-bezek live and bringing him to Jerusalem was a failure to obey God's clear command to put Canaanite leaders entirely to death.

notes.meaning: The men of Judah attacked the city of Jerusalem and captured it. They struck down its inhabitants and set the city ablaze. Although they conquered the city itself, the fortress on the hill held out longer. It was a significant early blow against a major Canaanite stronghold.

After taking Jerusalem, the soldiers of Judah pressed further into their territory. They fought the Canaanites living across three distinct regions: the rugged mountains, the dry southern desert called the Negev, and the western foothills. They were working to secure every part of the land God had given them. Faithful obedience tackles every challenge, whether in high hills or barren deserts.

Judah marched against the historic city of Hebron, which had once been named Kiriath-arba. There they defeated the three clan chiefs of the Anakites: Sheshai, Ahiman, and Talmai. These were the giant-like warriors who had terrified Israel's spies a generation earlier. God showed that faith can overcome the very giants that once seemed impossible.

From Hebron, the army advanced to attack the town of Debir. In earlier days, this town was called Kiriath-sepher, which means 'City of the Book' or 'City of Writing.' It was another fortified Anakite settlement nestled in the hill country. Judah continued to clear out the pagan settlements step by step.

Caleb offered his daughter Acsah in marriage to any brave man who would capture Kiriath-sepher. Caleb's nephew, Othniel, stepped forward in courage and took the town. Caleb kept his word and gave Acsah to him as his wife. Caleb inspired the next generation of leaders, and Othniel would later become Israel's first judge.

When Acsah arrived to marry Othniel, she urged him to ask her father for an additional field. As she met her father, she stepped down from her donkey to show deep respect and make a serious request. Caleb noticed her action and asked what she needed. She was bold and practical in seeking what would help her new family flourish.

Acsah asked Caleb for a special blessing of springs of water, since the land in the Negev was dry and barren. Caleb generously answered her prayer by giving her both upper and lower springs. This fresh water made the dry ground fertile and fruitful. In a similar way, God's people may come freely to their heavenly Father for the living water of His Spirit.

The Kenites were relatives of Moses' father-in-law who had travelled with Israel from the wilderness. They left their temporary home near Jericho, the 'City of Palms,' and moved south with Judah. They settled down peacefully in the wilderness near Arad among the people of Judah. God remained faithful to the promise made long before to welcome and bless this family.

Judah fulfilled its promise to Simeon by joining them to attack the town of Zephath. They completely destroyed the town and devoted it to the Lord. Because of this destruction, they renamed the place Hormah, which means 'devoted to ruin.' The two brother tribes honoured their agreement and completed what God commanded.

Judah also struck into Philistine territory along the Mediterranean coast and captured three major cities: Gaza, Ashkelon, and Ekron. These were heavily fortified coastal settlements with surrounding villages. Although Judah took them at this time, Israel failed to hold them permanently, and the Philistines soon regained control. Partial success quickly slips away when God's people do not finish what they started.

The Lord was with Judah, and they took firm hold of the mountains and hill towns. Down in the plains, however, they failed to drive out the Canaanites because the enemy possessed iron chariots. God was fully able to give them the plains, but Israel let fear of enemy weapons overcome their faith. When believers look at earthly obstacles instead of God's power, their progress stops.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: The traditional Latin and Douay-Rheims renderings describe these vehicles as scythed chariots armed with cutting blades.

notes.meaning: As Moses had promised decades earlier, the city and lands of Hebron were given to Caleb. Even in his old age, Caleb trusted God and drove out the three Anakite clans living there. Where others saw terrifying giants, Caleb saw an opportunity for God to show His power. Faithful obedience brings lasting reward just as God has said.

The tribe of Benjamin failed to drive out the pagan Jebusites who held the stronghold of Jerusalem. Instead of trusting God to remove them, Benjamin settled for letting the Jebusites live among them. This compromise lasted for centuries until the time of King David. Compromising with sin always creates problems that linger for future generations.

The tribes of Ephraim and Manasseh, known together as the house of Joseph, marched against the city of Bethel. The Lord was with them in their unified campaign, giving them strength for the battle. Before attacking, they sent scouts to inspect the town, which was anciently called Luz. God blesses His people when they work together in faith and wisdom.

The scouts spotted a man leaving the city and asked him to show them an entrance or weak spot in the defenses. In exchange, they promised to spare him and treat him kindly. The man pointed out the entrance, allowing Joseph's forces to take the city while keeping their word to spare his family. God honored the practical mercy shown to the man while fulfilling the judgment on Bethel.

After being spared, the man left the region and moved northward into the land of the Hittites. There he founded a brand new settlement and named it Luz after his former home. Unlike Rahab, who joined Israel and worshipped the true God, this man simply rebuilt his old pagan lifestyle elsewhere. Merely escaping judgment is not the same as turning one's heart to God.

The tribe of Manasseh failed to drive out the Canaanite residents of Beth-shean, Taanach, Dor, Ibleam, Megiddo, and their nearby villages. These strong fortress cities formed a chain across the fertile valleys of central Canaan. The Canaanites were determined to hold their ground, and Manasseh did not have the faith or resolve to remove them. When God's people lack spiritual determination, old enemies dig in deep.

When Israel grew stronger and more populous, they still did not drive out the Canaanites as the Lord commanded. Instead, they forced them to pay tribute and perform hard labor. Israel chose financial profit and easy convenience over wholehearted obedience to God's law. Choosing personal gain over God's commands always leads to spiritual decay.

The tribe of Ephraim also failed to clear out the Canaanites living in the city of Gezer. Instead, Ephraim allowed the Canaanites to continue living quietly right in their midst. Gezer remained an independent Canaanite center until the days of King Solomon. Small spiritual compromises soon become permanent fixtures in our lives.

The tribe of Zebulun failed to drive out the inhabitants of Kitron and Nahalol. The Canaanites continued to live among the Israelites, though Zebulun made them forced laborers. While Zebulun held some authority, they still refused to carry out God's full instruction. Halfway obedience is still disobedience in God's eyes.

The tribe of Asher failed to drive out the people of major Phoenician port cities such as Acco and Sidon. Asher's condition became even worse than the other tribes, because they ended up living as guests among the Canaanites who ruled the land. They completely lost the upper hand because they gave up the fight. When believers stop resisting worldly ways, the culture quickly begins to rule over them.

Naphtali also failed to expel the inhabitants of Beth-shemesh and Beth-anath, which were fortified centers of sun worship. Like Asher, Naphtali lived among the Canaanite population, though they eventually placed them under forced labor. Tolerating idol-worshipping communities right beside them exposed Israel to terrible temptations. Allowing ungodly influences near us will slowly erode our devotion to God.

The tribe of Dan suffered the worst defeat among all the tribes. The Amorites pushed the Danites back into the steep mountains and refused to let them come down into the fertile coastal plain. Dan lost almost their entire assigned inheritance because they could not overcome their enemies. Without relying on God's strength, His people are easily pushed out of their blessings.

The Amorites were determined to hold on to Mount Heres, Aijalon, and Shaalbim. Later on, the neighbouring house of Joseph grew strong enough to overpower them and put them to forced labor. Even then, the Amorites were never driven out, only made into tax-paying workers. Israel continued to prefer economic profit over the purity and holiness God required.

The territory of the Amorites stretched across southern Canaan, from the Scorpion Pass all the way past Sela. This note explains why the Amorites were so powerful and hard to conquer. They held a massive, well-defended region that pressed right up against Israel's borders. The chapter closes showing how incomplete Israel's conquest was because of their faltering faith.
